extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students (practitioners of patent litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria used by courts of equity when deciding injunctions, accounts of profits, inspections, and related remedial measures in patent-infringement litigation. Focuses on when equity will act vs send parties to law, and how monetary relief is measured and ordered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court discretion to grant injunctions vs sending to law
rubrics_metrics.description: The court is competent to grant an injunction simpliciter, but it is a question of convenience and the court must exercise a fair discretion whether to direct the parties to try the matter in a court of law where the legal question and facts can be better investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equity court may decline to grant or make final a perpetual injunction when there is an opportunity to have the question tried at law; the decision rests on convenience and sound judicial discretion, not on any absolute rule. Examples and citations (e.g., Stevens v. Keating; Russell v. Barnsley) illustrate that defendants are ordinarily afforded the opportunity to try the issue at law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice when validity is denied in answer (sending to law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant's answer positively denies the validity of the patent and prays for a trial by jury, the chancellor in England generally will not grant a final/perpetual injunction without sending the parties to law to have that question decided, though the rule is not absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This English practice is founded on convenience; courts of the United States are not uniformly so strict and sometimes decree final injunctions without a prior verdict (e.g., cases involving complex scientific or mechanical questions). The presence of a denial in the answer is a significant factor pushing toward trial at law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances permitting equity to decide facts and law without a jury verdict
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity may proceed to decide both questions of fact and law and grant a final injunction without a jury verdict when specific circumstances exist: the case has been set down for final hearing on exhibits and proofs; the court, after full hearing, feels no doubt on the issues; or a jury trial would be unduly time-consuming and unlikely to alter the court's conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider (1) whether the matter was fully submitted on proofs and exhibits, (2) whether the court is satisfied after hearing able counsel and the testimony, and (3) whether a jury trial would consume excessive time or be unlikely to produce a different result. The complexity of scientific or technical principles and potential jury incompetence to resolve them are relevant considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for dissolving an injunction on affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: On a motion on affidavits to dissolve an injunction, the defendant's proofs must overcome the equity of the bill and the evidence in its support; mere filing of an answer or affidavits casting doubt on validity will not displace the plaintiff's prima facie right provided the plaintiff has not unreasonably delayed and adduces auxiliary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion to dissolve may be made at any time; if a trial at law has been ordered or is pending the decision follows the same principles as in granting the injunction. Cases (e.g., Sparkman v. Higgins; Orr v. Merrill) supply precedent for these points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a trial at law or motions for a new trial on injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: After a trial at law, the equity court examines the result and will be governed by the position in which the plaintiff's right has been left; if proceedings at law are not final (e.g., a new trial is to be moved for) the court will not automatically continue or revive an injunction but will seek to leave parties in the situation causing the least inconvenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a verdict for plaintiff exists but a new trial has been or will be sought, the injunction may not be continued as a matter of course; the court may refuse or stand over injunction applications until the result of the new trial or related motions is known and may require defendants to keep accounts in the interim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core patent validity requirements (novelty, utility, intelligible specification, proper claiming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent instructions: first, the invention must be novel; secondly, it must be useful; thirdly, the specification must be intelligible; additionally, the specification must not attempt to cover more than the patentee is strictly entitled to claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility and intelligibility are typically matters for the jury as facts, while whether a specification overclaims (attempts to cover too much) is a question of law. A specification that claims more than the patentee is entitled to renders the patent ineffectual even to the extent of fair entitlement. Patents for new combinations or methods must clearly confine the claim to the new combination or application and not claim original invention of materials already known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding prejudice while right is tried (accounts instead of injunctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity aims to preserve to each party the benefit to which they may be entitled until the right is tried; instead of imposing an injunction that would cause substantial prejudice to a defendant, the court may direct the defendant to keep an account of profits and continue operations pending trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a plaintiff has acquiesced or permitted defendants to erect costly works, stopping the works by injunction can create greater injustice. Ordering an account (sometimes from the time works commenced) secures the plaintiff's remedy if successful while avoiding irreparable injury to the defendant's business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of inspectors/viewers for mutual inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: When infringement is to be tried at law, the court may order a mutual inspection of the plaintiff's and defendant's works; inspectors or viewers appointed under court direction are admitted as witnesses at the trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose is to enable parties to present evidence tending to prove or disprove infringement. If parties cannot agree on the persons to be appointed, the court will appoint them (cases: Morgan v. Seaward; Russell v. Cowley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering an account of profits and its usual application
rubrics_metrics.description: An account of profits is sometimes ordered in lieu of granting or continuing an injunction and is always ordered when a perpetual injunction is decreed (unless the amount would be very small). It secures that, if the plaintiff is ultimately found entitled, the defendant's profits while using the invention are available for redress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts are ordered on the principle that a plaintiff is more secure of ample justice if the defendant's profits are accounted for while the defendant continues use and makes new contracts; an account may also be ordered if the injunction is dissolved to avoid irreparable injury to the defendant's business (cases: Hill v. Thompson; Crossley v. Derby Gas Light Company).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and form of decree for profits (master's reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When validity is established, a decree will direct taking an account of all profits made by the defendant in violation of the patent (by making, using, or vending the articles named in the bill); the master may take the account down to the time of hearing and the decree may extend to articles made during the patent's existence even if unsold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proper form of decree explicitly directs an account of profits; the master is not strictly limited to the decree date but should follow the court's instructions and the prayer of the bill in scope (see Crossley v. Beverley; Rubber Co. v. Goodyear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of profits limited to actual gains (Livingston v. Woodworth principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: An account of profits granted by equity comprises only the profits actually made by the defendant, not profits which he might have made with reasonable diligence, nor interest from the date of filing the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court reversed broader measures that awarded conjectural or hypothetical profits; masters must not compute profits on speculative assumptions ungoverned by evidence. Consent decrees and instructions to masters are to be interpreted in light of the prayer of the bill and equitable principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of consent decrees and master's authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A consent decree or decretal order is to be interpreted by its clear language; reference to a master is not an arbitration that binds parties beyond the prayer of the bill, and courts will review, recommit, or set aside master's reports that depart from the decree or contain conjectural awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that defendants are not bound by an open-ended consent to any form of account: the account consented to is the account prayed for by the bill (i.e., actual gains/profits). Masters' reports are subject to exceptions and review; the court must ensure that instructions to the master conform to equitable principles and the bill's prayer (Livingston v. Woodworth).
